subject: Climate & Environment
title: Energy Access and Equity
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Energy Access and Equity.

hook.text: About 770 million people still have no access to electricity at all.

buildup.text: Most live in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia — regions with abundant sunlight.

discovery.text: Solar microgrids can bring power to remote villages without building expensive grid lines.

twist.text: Rich nations used fossil fuels to develop. Now they ask poor nations to skip that step.

climax.text: Clean energy leapfrogging is possible — like mobile phones skipping landlines.

punchline.text: The energy transition must lift everyone, not just the connected.

quiz.question: How many people worldwide lack access to electricity?

details.summary: About 675 million people still lack access to electricity, mostly in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. Decentralized renewable energy systems like solar mini-grids and pay-as-you-go solar kits offer a path to electrification that bypasses expensive centralized grid infrastructure.
details.whyItMatters: Energy access is fundamental to health, education, and economic opportunity. Off-grid renewables can reach underserved communities faster and more affordably than traditional grid expansion.
takeaways: Roughly 675 million people have no electricity access
Solar mini-grids offer faster electrification than grid extension
Pay-as-you-go models make solar affordable for low-income users

faq.question: What is a solar mini-grid?
faq.answer: A solar mini-grid is a small, localized power system with solar panels, batteries, and a distribution network serving a village or community. It operates independently of the national grid and can provide reliable electricity to hundreds of households and businesses.

faq.question: How does pay-as-you-go solar work?
faq.answer: Companies provide solar home systems on credit, with payments made via mobile money in small daily or weekly installments. If payments stop, the system is remotely locked. Once fully paid, the user owns the system. This model has brought power to millions in East Africa.
